query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under sustained loading at creep-relevant temperatures, FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers progressively deform plastically because localized breakdown of interfacial short-range order (SRO) lowers the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation and glide.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer system composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloys that exhibits pronounced interfacial SRO, significant lattice distortion from compositional complexity, and a well-preserved layered architecture.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary deposition parameters or post-deposition thermal treatments to tune the degree of interfacial SRO, then subject the samples to in situ creep tests under controlled stress and moderate-to-elevated temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Sustained mechanical loading at temperatures where atomic diffusion is appreciable but the nanoscale multilayer structure remains intact; comparisons are made between multilayers with intact (baseline) and intentionally degraded interfacial SRO.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial short-range order (SRO) and its associated lattice distortions arising from compositional complexity and misfit between layers.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained stress, local regions at the interfaces experience a breakdown or reorganization of SRO, which reduces the barrier to dislocation nucleation and increases dislocation mobility. This accelerated dislocation activity leads to enhanced localized plastic deformation (creep).
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with intentionally degraded interfacial SRO will exhibit higher creep strain rates and increased localized dislocation activity near the interfaces when compared to baseline samples with preserved SRO under identical loading and temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Multilayer coatings with well-maintained interfacial SRO and controlled lattice distortions are expected to show lower creep rates and more homogeneous deformation under sustained loading.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under moderate-to-high temperature creep conditions in the nanoscale multilayer architecture; under extreme temperatures or stresses where diffusion creep or phase transformations prevail, alternative deformation mechanisms may become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contribution of interfacial SRO degradation relative to other potential creep mechanisms in these highly complex systems remains uncertain and requires further empirical quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers: one with optimized processing to retain high interfacial SRO, and another where post-deposition thermal treatments intentionally degrade the interfacial SRO. Subject both sets to in situ creep tests under identical stress and moderate-to-elevated temperature conditions while monitoring dislocation activity and SRO evolution using high-resolution TEM, in situ diffraction techniques, and quantitative spectroscopy.
measurements: Dislocation density and spatial distribution (especially near interfaces)
Quantitative assessment of interfacial SRO via diffraction or spectroscopic measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with intentionally degraded interfacial SRO do not exhibit a significantly higher creep rate or show no increase in localized dislocation activity compared to the baseline samples with intact SRO, then the hypothesis that SRO breakdown governs progressive plastic deformation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High or medium- entropy alloys (HEAs/MEAs) are multi-principal element alloys with equal atomic elemental composition, some of which have shown record-breaking mechanical performance. However, the link between short-range order (SRO) and the exceptional mechanical properties of these alloys has remained elusive. The local destruction of SRO by dislocation glide has been predicted to lead to a rejuvenated state with increased entropy and free energy, creating softer zones within the matrix and planar fault boundaries that enhance the ductility, but this has not been verified. Here, we integrate in situ nanomechanical testing with energy-filtered four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) and directly observe the rejuvenation during cyclic mechanical loading in single crystal CrCoNi at room temperature. Surprisingly, stacking faults (SFs) and twin boundaries (TBs) are reversible in initial cycles but become irreversible after a thousand cycles, indicating SF energy reduction and rejuvenation. The frequent changes of atom type and size cause a large atomic-scale lattice distortion in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), resulting in excellent mechanical properties, such as great strength and good ductility (), and high fracture toughness (, ). In particular, refractory MPEA (RMPEA) shows high strength at elevated temperatures (), but its low room-temperature ductility hinders the wide applications (). Recently, non-screw dislocation slip plays an important contribution to plastic deformation in RMPEA () and attracts a lot of great attention to break through this dilemma (). Additionally, the differences of the electronic interactions lead to the existence of preference or avoidance in the atom bonding and then produce chemical short-range order (SRO) to reduce the free energy of the system confirmed by experiments (). At this point, the alloy’s dislocation activation volume V* is 0.21 b3 (Figure 11), which is typically associated with the non-uniform nucleation of dislocations, and creep deformation occurs through direct atom–vacancy exchange []. These findings suggest that the creep deformation mechanism of the same alloy can vary under different loading rates. In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.

A previous experimental study showed that the high strength of a CoCu0.7FeNiAl0.3 HEA arose primarily from grain-boundary strengthening and dislocation-strengthening mechanisms. In a subsequent MD study on the same HEA, it was found that when dislocation nucleation and emission were suppressed, strain-induced phase transformations from the FCC to BCC phase occurred. The variation of the BCC volume fraction (phase transformation) with strain during tensile deformation is exhibited in Fig. 2f for the no-SRO and SRO samples under 300 K tension. In summary, the study reveals that the maximum strength and critical grain size can be manipulated by tuning the degree of chemical SRO, signifying the nontrivial role of local chemical ordering on the ultimate strength of MPEAs. As the salient feature of MPEAs, the presence of SRO considerably affects deformation microstructure and local plastic strain, originating from its effects on SF energy increase and diffuse antiphase boundary development. As a result, the volume fracture of deformation hcp atoms is decreased to compensate the increased SF energy, and plastic strain is more localized to embrace slip-mediated SRO destruction and glide plane softening. decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys applied dislocation‐based deformation models from conventional metallic systems, but soon it became clear that the severe lattice distortion and the presence of short‐range order (SRO) in HEAs altered typical dislocation behavior. Studies such as PMC4949441 revealed that in high-entropy materials the mechanics of dislocation slip (e.g. the absence of dislocation dissociation due to high antiphase-boundary energies) could be significantly modified. Later, investigations (e.g. PMC10873362) started to expose how dislocation glide can locally disrupt SRO, leading to a ‘rejuvenated’ state that manifests as planar defects. However, while preliminary FCC/BCC multilayer experiments hinted at unusual creep behavior, the precise way in which interfacial SRO degradation and lattice misfit between alternating layers control the evolution from elastic to progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear whether progressive plastic deformation (i.e. creep) in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by a gradual breakdown or reorganization of SRO at and near the interfaces, which could enhance local dislocation nucleation and motion. The controlled comparison linking interfacial SRO (and its evolution under sustained stress) to the specific onset and rate of creep deformation in these complex, multilayered systems has not been established.
decision.lever: Systematically tune and characterize the interfacial short‐range order and lattice distortion (e.g., by modifying deposition parameters or post‐deposition thermal treatments) while performing in situ creep tests to monitor the emergence of localized deformation events.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of recognizing that in HEAs, and particularly in multilayers with compositional complexity, the interfacial SRO plays a key role in mediating dislocation activity and plasticity. By controlling the degree of SRO at the layer interfaces, one can directly test whether its progressive degradation is what governs sustained creep deformation. This lever builds on prior evidence that dislocation glide disrupts SRO (as seen in PMC10873362) while addressing the gap of establishing a controlled, comparative baseline in multilayer architectures.
